Thiocyanate coordination mode

Words: 86 Articles: 1
Thiocyanate OurBigBook.com
thiocyanate can coordinate through nitrogen, sulfur, or both ends, and can bridge several metal centres. A linkage label specifies donor atoms, whereas the bridging index μn​ specifies the number of connected metals. A short C–N bond and long C–S bond favour an N≡C−S− description; greater C–S and smaller C–N bond orders give more −N=C=S character. Internal distances alone need not determine how many metals are attached.

Lipid

Chemical substance OurBigBook.com
Lipids are a chemically diverse family of chemical substances, conventionally associated with biological origin and solubility in nonpolar solvents. They include triglycerides, phospholipids, and cholesterol. The name does not specify one molecular formula, one repeating monomer, or one kind of polymer. Some lipids have both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions rather than being uniformly nonpolar. See IUPAC Gold Book: lipids.
Structure explains the different jobs. A triglyceride has three fatty acid-derived acyl groups attached to glycerol and serves as an energy store. A typical glycerophospholipid instead combines two such chains with a phosphate-containing head, making it an amphiphile suited to a lipid bilayer. Cholesterol has a different structure and also contributes to cell membrane properties. Thus a lipid is a chemical building material, while a lipid bilayer is an organization of many molecules. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 3.3: lipid structures and functions.

Phospholipid

Words: 790 Articles: 13
Lipid OurBigBook.com
Phospholipids are lipids containing a phosphate group as part of their structure linked by covalent bonds. The familiar membrane-forming phospholipids are amphiphilic: a hydrophilic head region with chemical polarity coexists with a hydrophobic, largely nonpolar hydrocarbon region. These descriptions refer to different parts of the same molecule, not to two separate substances. See IUPAC Gold Book: phospholipids and IUPAC Gold Book: amphiphilic.
A typical two-chain glycerophospholipid provides a useful example: a glycerol scaffold carries two fatty acid-derived acyl groups through ester linkages, plus a phosphate-containing head region. Phosphatidylcholine is one example. This scaffold describes an important subclass, rather than all phospholipids: sphingomyelin has a different backbone, and even glycerophospholipids need not all have two acyl groups. See IUPAC–IUB, Nomenclature of Lipids (1976), Lip-1.5 and Lip-2.1–2.6.
Polar does not mean negatively charged overall. At near-neutral pH, phosphatidylcholine is zwitterionic: its phosphate region carries negative electric charge and its choline region positive electric charge, with zero net electric charge for the molecule. Counting those opposite charges gives (−1)+(+1)=0; it does not remove their local interactions with water. See Lodish et al., Molecular Cell Biology: membrane lipids.
In a lipid bilayer, two membrane leaflets orient their hydrophilic heads toward the water on either side and their hydrophobic chains toward the shared interior. The hydrophobic effect helps explain this organization through the free energy of the water and lipids together. It is not a special repulsive chemical bond between chains and water. Which organization is favored also depends on molecular geometry, temperature, concentration, and the surrounding chemical solution; a phospholipid label alone does not guarantee a lipid bilayer. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: the lipid bilayer.
This organization supplies a flexible barrier for compartments. A fluid lipid bilayer allows lipids to undergo diffusion within each membrane leaflet; barrier function therefore coexists with motion of molecules, as in the fluid mosaic model. It is not completely impermeable: small nonpolar molecules such as molecular oxygen and carbon dioxide cross much more readily than ions. In a cell membrane, ion channels and other membrane transport proteins provide selective routes; the existing membrane transport article explains their driving forces. See Alberts et al.: principles of membrane transport.
In 1925, E. Gorter and F. Grendel extracted lipids from red blood cells and compared the surface area of a one-molecule-thick film on water with the estimated total surface area of the red blood cells. Their table gave ratios near two, supporting a two-layer covering; they also proposed heads facing the aqueous surroundings on both sides. The inference depends on recovering the relevant lipids, estimating the red blood cell surface area correctly, and comparing compatible packing in the film and the cell membrane. It was indirect evidence, not an image of the lipid bilayer. The paper itself notes possible losses during evaporation. See Gorter and Grendel, On Bimolecular Layers of Lipoids on the Chromocytes of the Blood, Journal of Experimental Medicine 41 (1925), 439–443.

Carbohydrate

Words: 2k Articles: 26
Chemical substance OurBigBook.com
Carbohydrates are a family of chemical substances encompassing monosaccharides, combinations of monosaccharides, and their derivatives. Glucose is a small carbohydrate; cellulose is a long-chain polysaccharide. Deoxyribose illustrates why composition alone does not define the family: replacing a hydroxy group in ribose by hydrogen still leaves a carbohydrate. See IUPAC Gold Book: carbohydrates.
Many familiar monosaccharides have a molecular formula of the form Cn​H2n​On​, equivalently Cn​(H2​O)n​. This explains the historical name, “hydrate of carbon”, but does not mean the molecule consists of carbon mixed with intact water molecules. Nor is it a universal formula: deoxyribose has C5​H10​O4​. The family is defined through chemical structure and relationships, not that ratio. See IUPAC's definition and origin of the name carbohydrate.
The useful surprise is the variety of roles obtainable from related building blocks. Glucose participates in metabolism, ribose forms part of RNA, and linked glucose units make structural cellulose in a plant cell wall. Understanding carbohydrates therefore connects cellular energy, molecular information, and material structure. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: the chemical components of a cell.

Sugar

Words: 2k Articles: 13
Carbohydrate OurBigBook.com
In chemical usage, sugars commonly means small carbohydrates, including single-unit monosaccharides and two-unit disaccharides. Glucose, ribose, and deoxyribose are monosaccharides. Cellulose is instead a polysaccharide assembled from many glucose units. The distinction counts chemically linked units; it does not classify every carbohydrate by sweetness or biological role. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 3.2: carbohydrates.
A useful first description of a monosaccharide asks how many carbon chemical atoms it contains and what its open-chain structure is. Ribose is an aldopentose, a five-carbon aldehyde sugar; glucose is an aldohexose, with six carbon chemical atoms. A Fischer projection then records the stereochemistry, information missing from the molecular formula. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, 25.1: carbohydrate classification.

Ribose (C5​H10​O5​)

Words: 248
Sugar OurBigBook.com
Ribose is a monosaccharide with molecular formula C5​H10​O5​. Its biologically familiar form is D-ribose, an aldopentose whose open-chain Fischer projection has CHO at the top, CH2​OH at the bottom, and hydroxy groups on the right at C2, C3, and C4. The opposite horizontal substituents are hydrogen. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, 25.3: D-ribose and D-glucose configurations.
Read the drawing by counting groups: CHO contributes CHO, three CHOH groups contribute C3​H6​O3​, and CH2​OH contributes CH3​O. Their sum is C5​H10​O5​. The count checks composition; the right/right/right pattern additionally specifies the stereochemistry of D-ribose.
In RNA, ribose occurs as a ring within each nucleotide, joining a nucleobase to the phosphate-linked backbone. Its C2 position retains a hydroxy group, unlike deoxyribose in DNA. In a nucleotide, the sugar positions carry primes, so this is C2′. See Alberts et al.: nucleotide sugars in RNA and DNA. Free ribose in water is also predominantly cyclic, with several ring forms in chemical equilibrium and very little open-chain form; the Fischer projection is valuable for comparing configurations, not for estimating their abundances. See Mason et al., The Conformation of a Ribose Derivative in Aqueous Solution: A Neutron Scattering and Molecular Dynamics Study (2013), introduction.

Deoxyribose (C5​H10​O4​)

Words: 203
Sugar OurBigBook.com
In the usual DNA context, deoxyribose means 2-deoxy-D-ribose, a five-carbon monosaccharide with molecular formula C5​H10​O4​. Relative to D-ribose, the hydroxy group at C2 is replaced by hydrogen. The locant 2 matters: it identifies which position loses its oxygen. See Favre and Powell, IUPAC Blue Book, P-102.5.3: deoxy sugars and IUPAC: nucleic acids and their component sugars.
The paired Fischer projections in ribose make the change concrete. C2 has hydrogen on both sides, while C3 and C4 retain their hydroxy groups on the right. C2 is therefore not a stereocenter: exchanging its two identical hydrogen substituents cannot produce a distinct configuration. The unchanged C3 and C4 still carry stereochemical information.
Replacing OH by H removes one oxygen but leaves the total hydrogen count unchanged: the hydrogen belonging to the removed hydroxy group is replaced by a hydrogen bonded directly to carbon. Thus C5​H10​O5​ becomes C5​H10​O4​. This comparison describes structures, rather than a complete chemical reaction or its mechanism.
In DNA, deoxyribose is incorporated as a ring in each nucleotide, with phosphate connections building the backbone. Its C2′ bears hydrogen where RNA's ribose bears a hydroxy group. This small local difference lets the sugar structure identify the two kinds of nucleic acid; the nucleobases supply their sequence information. See Alberts et al.: nucleotides as the subunits of DNA and RNA.

Glucose (C6​H12​O6​)

Words: 266
Sugar OurBigBook.com
Glucose is a monosaccharide with molecular formula C6​H12​O6​. Its familiar biological form, D-glucose, is an aldohexose. In the open-chain Fischer projection, CHO is at the top and CH2​OH at the bottom; the hydroxy groups at C2, C3, C4, and C5 point right, left, right, right. This full pattern distinguishes D-glucose from other six-carbon aldehyde sugars. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, 25.4: configurations of the aldoses.
The molecular formula can be checked directly: one CHO group, four CHOH groups, and one CH2​OH group give six carbon, twelve hydrogen, and six oxygen chemical atoms. All four interior carbon positions are stereocenters in this open-chain structure. Neither their orientations nor the arrangement of chemical bonds can be recovered from the molecular formula alone.
In water, glucose exists mainly in six-membered rings in chemical equilibrium with a small amount of open-chain glucose. Ring closure connects the hydroxy group at C5 to the aldehyde carbon at C1; the ring contains five carbon chemical atoms and one oxygen, with C6 outside it. No chemical atoms are lost, so the molecular formula remains C6​H12​O6​. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, 25.5: cyclic structures of monosaccharides.
Glucose is useful both as a substrate in cellular metabolism and as a building block of polysaccharides. Cellulose chains assembled from glucose units help support plant cell walls. The same small sugar thus connects chemical fuel to a structural material; its role depends on how it is transformed or linked. See Cooper, The Cell: A Molecular Approach, the molecular composition of cells.

Monosaccharide

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Sugar OurBigBook.com
A monosaccharide is a single-unit carbohydrate that cannot be split into smaller sugars by hydrolysis. Ribose, deoxyribose, and glucose are examples. The unit is a whole molecule containing many chemical atoms; a disaccharide instead contains two linked monosaccharide units.[ref]
Classification combines carbon count with open-chain connectivity. An aldose has an aldehyde group; a ketose has a ketone group. Thus glucose is an aldohexose, while fructose is a six-carbon ketose. These names describe the open-chain reference forms even when cyclic forms predominate in water.[ref]
Check the distinction by counting the groups in the drawings. Open-chain glucose contains one CHO, four CHOH and one CH2​OH group. Open-chain fructose contains two CH2​OH, three CHOH and one C=O group. The respective hydrogen totals are 1+4(2)+3=12 and 2(3)+3(2)=12; each structure also has six carbon and six oxygen chemical atoms. Their shared molecular formula C6​H12​O6​ therefore cannot identify the carbonyl group position or the stereochemistry.
The beauty is that a familiar sugar name can embrace an interconverting family of forms. Monosaccharide ring-chain interconversion connects those drawings to mutarotation, a change visible with polarimetry. Spatial arrangement also matters to biology: an enzyme's active site encounters a particular arrangement of hydroxy groups, rather than merely an inventory of chemical atoms. The existing enzyme and chirality articles explain that recognition principle.
Aldopentose
Words: 103
Monosaccharide OurBigBook.com
An aldopentose is a five-carbon aldose: its open-chain reference form has an aldehyde group at C1. Ribose is an example; deoxyribose is its 2-deoxy derivative.[ref]
For the unmodified open-chain aldopentose skeleton, count one CHO, three CHOH and one CH2​OH group: C5​H10​O5​. The three interior carbon positions, C2–C4, are stereocenters. Each allows two configurations, giving 23=8 stereoisomers, grouped into four enantiomer pairs. The unlike chain ends prevent a meso compound identification. D-ribose selects the right/right/right hydroxy group pattern in the Fischer projection; the word aldopentose alone does not select that pattern. Compare the existing ribose and deoxyribose diagrams for the separate question of which oxygen is present.
Aldohexose
Words: 83
Monosaccharide OurBigBook.com
An aldohexose is a six-carbon aldose: its open-chain reference form has an aldehyde group at C1. Glucose is an example.[ref]
The unmodified open-chain skeleton has four stereocenters, C2–C5, giving 24=16 stereoisomers, or eight enantiomer pairs. Fixing the C5 hydroxy group on the right leaves 23=8 D forms; D-glucose's right/left/right/right pattern selects one. An aldohexose label therefore specifies less than a particular sugar name, and a molecular formula specifies less still. The existing glucose article checks its chemical atom inventory; monosaccharide ring-chain interconversion follows those same numbered carbon positions into a ring.
Monosaccharide ring-chain interconversion
Words: 667 Articles: 1
Monosaccharide OurBigBook.com
In water, D-glucose mainly occupies cyclic forms. The C5 hydroxy group adds to the C1 aldehyde, forming a cyclic hemiacetal; reversible opening restores the aldehyde. Reclosure can give either anomer. Their changing proportions cause mutarotation, the approach of optical rotation to an equilibrium value. This pathway involves changing chemical bonds, rather than simply rotating a hydroxy group about a single chemical bond.[ref]
In this conventional Haworth projection, C5's CH2​OH group points up. The alpha anomer's C1 hydroxy group points down, on the opposite face; the beta anomer's points up, on the same face. C2/C3/C4 retain down/up/down hydroxy groups. These are above/below relationships to a reference ring plane, not a claim that the ring is physically flat.[ref]
The anomeric carbon is C1, the existing carbonyl group carbon that becomes a new stereocenter; no extra carbon chemical atom appears. The two anomers differ at that centre while retaining the other configurations.[ref]
Trace the ring as C1–C2–C3–C4–C5–O5–C1, where O5 denotes the oxygen originally in the C5 hydroxy group. It contains five carbon chemical atoms and one oxygen; C6 remains attached outside the ring. The C1 carbonyl group oxygen becomes the C1 hydroxy group oxygen. This accounts for every oxygen: O5 in the ring and five hydroxy groups at C1, C2, C3, C4 and C6. Ring closure preserves C6​H12​O6​. A six-membered ring and a six-carbon sugar are thus different counts.
Glucose mutarotation experiment
Words: 365
Monosaccharide ring-chain interconversion OurBigBook.com
An endpoint experiment uses a polarimeter with a 1.0dm sample cell and supplied 4%, 6% and 8% D-glucose chemical solutions. Collect about 15mL of each. Fill the cell first with distilled water, dry its windows, move bubbles to the air trap, and retain its orientation. Scan light intensity against polarimeter analyzer angle through 360∘. The protocol fits a Gaussian function to the upper third of a symmetric peak to locate its maximum. Rinse with the next sample, repeat for each glucose chemical solution, and subtract the water maximum's angle from each sample maximum. This is an operational peak-location method; the Gaussian function is not the physical transmission law.[ref]
The existing optical activity and polarimetry articles explain the apparatus, Malus's law and instrument limitations. For an extension that observes mutarotation in time, freshly dissolve a specified crystalline anomer, record the mixing time, and repeat the optical rotation readout at fixed concentration, path length, wavelength and recorded temperature. Keep pH consistent and record the delay before the first reading. These are proposed additions to the endpoint protocol, not its published steps or a claim of measured results. Recheck the water blank, repeat the preparation, and compare with a separately equilibrated portion under the same conditions. A stable endpoint alone does not show the time evolution.
Interpret each concentration separately. If θ is blank-corrected optical rotation, l is path length and c is total glucose mass concentration, first calculate specific rotation r=θ/(lc). In an additive two-anomer approximation, let rα​,rβ​ be reference specific rotations under the same conditions and xα​ the mole fraction of alpha within that pair. Equal molar masses make its mass fraction equal to xα​, so
r=xα​rα​+(1−xα​)rβ​,xα​=rα​−rβ​r−rβ​​.
(1)
This is a population estimate from an assumed response model, not direct imaging of an anomer. For a simple consistency check, doubling c at fixed l and unchanged composition doubles θ in this model while leaving r unchanged. Averaging raw optical rotations at different concentrations would fail this test; normalize first.
Changing temperature, pH, contamination, incomplete dissolution, window stress, bubbles or instrumental drift can imitate or obscure a changing signal. Reference specific rotations must match the sample conditions. Minor open-chain and other ring forms limit the two-anomer approximation; a single optical rotation cannot separately determine every population. Also, these anomers are diastereomers, not an enantiomer pair: the equal-and-opposite cancellation formula for enantiomeric excess does not apply.

Chemical formula

Words: 491 Articles: 4
Chemical substance OurBigBook.com
A chemical formula uses symbols of chemical elements and numerical subscripts to record composition. In the molecular formula H2​O of water, the subscript 2 counts two hydrogen chemical atoms, and the omitted subscript after O means one oxygen chemical atom. A molecular formula describes one molecule; a chemical formula need not describe a discrete molecule.
Read a preceding coefficient separately from the subscripts. One H2​O contains two hydrogen and one oxygen chemical atom; 2H2​O contains four hydrogen and two oxygen chemical atoms distributed between two water molecules. In H2​O2​, the second subscript instead puts two oxygen chemical atoms into each hydrogen peroxide molecule. Thus 2H2​O=H2​O2​: the coefficient scales the whole chemical formula, while a subscript specifies its composition. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, §2.4: chemical formulas.
For crystalline NaCl, the chemical formula specifies a 1:1 ratio of sodium ions Na+ to chlorine ions Cl−. Its formula unit is the accounting entity; the ordinary crystal is an extended arrangement of ions, rather than a collection of discrete NaCl molecules. Specifying the entity matters when assigning an amount of substance. See formula unit and 2.6 Ionic and Molecular Compounds (§2.6: ionic and molecular compounds).
A molecular formula gives an atom inventory, not the full arrangement of chemical bonds or the molecular geometry. For example, C6​H12​O6​ counts six carbon, twelve hydrogen, and six oxygen chemical atoms in a glucose molecule, but does not specify the pattern shown by its Fischer projection. Different structures can share a molecular formula. This compact inventory is useful for chemical equation accounting precisely because it leaves the structural detail to other representations.
The choice of letters has an early explanation in Jöns Jacob Berzelius, Essay on the Cause of Chemical Proportions (1813–1814), §III, transcribed by Carmen Giunta: letters made chemical signs easier to write and print, and formulas compressed information about composition. His numerical notation differed from modern subscripts; the lasting idea was to make proportions readable in ordinary text.

Amino acid

Words: 2k Articles: 19
Carboxylic acid OurBigBook.com
An amino acid combines carboxylic acid and amine functionality in the same molecule; the name alone does not specify their separation. An alpha-amino acid has its amino nitrogen attached to the carbon immediately adjacent to the carboxyl carbon, the amino acid alpha carbon. For example, H2​N−CH2​−COOH is glycine, whereas H2​N−CH2​−CH2​−COOH has an extra intervening carbon and is not an alpha-amino acid. These chemical formulas describe connectivity, not the predominant protonation state in water.
Most common proteinogenic amino acids share the skeleton H2​N−CH(R)−COOH, with R the amino acid side chain. In glycine, R is hydrogen; in alanine, R=CH3​. Proline is a useful exception to the displayed primary-amine skeleton: its amino nitrogen is part of a ring and has a second carbon substituent. The shared backbone permits assembly into polypeptides, while different amino acid side chains give the resulting proteins diverse chemistry. [ref]
In a chemical solution, protonation changes the electric charges without changing this backbone. Free glycine near neutral pH is predominantly H3​N+−CH2​−COO−, a zwitterion. Its positive and negative groups are joined within one molecule; zero net electric charge does not mean absence of local electric charges, nor does it mean the uncharged drawing H2​N−CH2​−COOH predominates. Glycine protonation explains how lowering or raising pH changes the balance. [ref]
Building a protein joins the carboxyl carbon of one amino acid to the amino nitrogen of another through a peptide bond, an amide linkage. The formal net condensation loses the elements of water; cellular translation uses activated substrates at a ribosome, rather than simply mixing free amino acids in water. Incorporated units are amino acid residues. The interior amide groups no longer have the same acid/base behavior as the two free terminal groups of glycine, so its free-molecule glycine titration cannot be copied independently at every chain position. [ref]
Chirality distinguishes most common proteinogenic amino acids from glycine. The other nineteen members of the conventional twenty have a stereocenter at their amino acid alpha carbon; ordinary translation incorporates their L forms. Glycine's two identical hydrogen substituents make it achiral. Thus being an amino acid, or even an alpha-amino acid, does not by itself imply chirality. [ref]

Glycine protonation
Words: 969 Articles: 3
Alpha-amino acid OurBigBook.com
The three principal aqueous glycine forms differ by loss of one proton at each step:
H3​N+−CH2​−COOH+H2​OH3​N+−CH2​−COO−+H2​O​⇌H3​N+−CH2​−COO−+H3​O+,⇌H2​N−CH2​−COO−+H3​O+.​
(2)
Call these glycine forms G+, G0 and G−, respectively: a cation, a zwitterion and an anion, with net electric charges +e, 0 and −e, where e is the elementary charge. G0 specifically denotes the zwitterion, not an uncharged amino/carboxyl drawing. The first dissociation removes the carboxyl proton; the second removes a proton from the positively charged nitrogen. The chemical equilibrium changes are reversible, not three permanently separate kinds of glycine. [ref]
For all calculations and both diagrams here, explicitly stipulate the pKa values pKa1​=2.35 and pKa2​=9.78. These are illustrative model inputs, not measurements from the glycine titration experiment or a claim of universal constants. Actual acid dissociation constants depend on temperature and on the convention used for thermodynamic activity; apparent concentration-based values also depend on ionic strength. For comparison, the inspected textbook tabulates 2.34 and 9.60 for glycine, which would give a different isoelectric point. [ref]
Glycine speciation model
Words: 149
Glycine protonation OurBigBook.com
In an ideal aqueous chemical solution, set h=[H3​O+]/c∘=10−pH, with c∘=1molL−1, and approximate activity coefficients by one. Put K1​=10−2.35 and K2​=10−9.78 for the stipulated dimensionless acid dissociation constants. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives the adjacent-state ratios
[G+][G0]​=hK1​​,[G0][G−]​=hK2​​.
(3)
With analytical concentration CT​=[G+]+[G0]+[G−], normalization gives the three fractions and mean electric charge in units of the elementary charge:
D=h2+K1​h+K1​K2​,α+​=Dh2​,α0​=DK1​h​,α−​=DK1​K2​​,zˉ=α+​−α−​.
(4)
All three fractions are nonnegative and sum to one. At pH 7, the model gives about 99.832% zwitterion, 0.00224% cation and 0.1657% anion; zˉ≈−0.00163. Predominantly zwitterionic therefore need not mean exactly at the isoelectric point.
Setting zˉ=0 requires h2=K1​K2​. Taking the logarithm yields
pI=2pKa1​+pKa2​​=22.35+9.78​=6.065.
(5)
At this model isoelectric point, α+​=α−​≈0.0001927 and α0​≈0.9996146: about 0.0193% of each charged form remains. At either pKa, the relevant adjacent fractions are equal, but the third fraction is not mathematically zero. This three-state model neglects the minor uncharged form H2​N−CH2​−COOH; macroscopic pKa values alone do not determine its fraction separately from the zwitterion.
Glycine titration
Words: 596 Articles: 1
Glycine protonation OurBigBook.com
Adding sodium hydroxide to acidified glycine successively removes its two titratable protons. Two broad buffer solution regions appear around the two pKa values, separated by a steep pH rise near the isoelectric point. This is useful evidence for two separated acid-base chemistry steps even though the changing chemical species are invisible. In the approximation that added hydroxide only changes glycine protonation, b=1−zˉ is the added base amount of substance per initial amount of substance of glycine. Then b≈0.5, 1 and 1.5 correspond to pKa1​, pI and pKa2​; endpoints are not exactly pure chemical species. [ref]
For the solid-curve model, start with nG​=0.00200mol of glycine in V0​=0.0200L and exactly nG​ of fully dissociated hydrochloric acid; this fixes the chloride inventory, but does not force every glycine molecule to remain G+. Let the sodium hydroxide concentration be CB​=0.100molL−1 and b=nNaOH​/nG​. Assume volume is additive and no other ions are present; stipulate Kw​=10−14 for self-ionization of water at a temperature of 25∘C. Then
V=V0​+CB​bnG​​,CT​=VnG​​,[Na+]=bCT​,[Cl−]=CT​.
(6)
Balancing all positive and negative electric charges requires
c∘(h−hKw​​)+CT​(b+zˉ−1)=0.
(7)
Solving this equation gives the solid curve. It remains finite at b=0 and beyond b=2, where ignoring free hydronium and hydroxide would fail. At the first pKa, the full model gives b≈0.436, rather than 0.5: appreciable free hydronium makes that half-equivalent shortcut inaccurate. At the second pKa, b≈1.502. Known acid inventory, dilution, and thermodynamic activity assumptions are therefore part of any quantitative interpretation, not optional corrections inferred from the curve's shape.
Glycine titration experiment
Words: 325
Glycine titration OurBigBook.com
The Amrita Virtual Lab procedure uses 0.1molL−1 glycine, hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, two burettes, a pH meter, beaker and stirrer. A pipette transfers 20mL of glycine into a 100mL beaker. Calibrate the meter with standard buffer solutions at pH 4, 7 and 10, then record the starting pH. Add hydrochloric acid in 0.3mL increments, recording pH after each addition until 1.6. Rinse the electrode in distilled water, take a separate fresh 20mL portion, and add sodium hydroxide in 0.3mL increments until pH 12.5. Its observed readout is paired added volume and pH, plotted as an acid-base titration curve; it does not measure each glycine form directly. [ref]
These are two titrations from the starting glycine chemical solution, rather than the single acidified-sample protocol assumed by the solid curve in glycine titration. Retain each portion's initial volume and the signed added acid/base amount of substance; do not concatenate raw burette readings and assume the result begins at b=0. For this procedure's 0.00200mol of glycine, each 0.3mL addition supplies 0.000030mol of acid or base, a 0.015 increment relative to the glycine inventory. This calculated resolution is not a reported measurement.
Useful additional controls are a fresh repeat portion, independently checked acid/base concentrations, a water blank, and a calibration-check buffer solution after the run. Stir without striking the glass electrode, keep its sensing region immersed and wait for stable readings; record temperature and background salts. Reduce addition size near a steep pH change. These are suggested controls for testing the model, beyond the published steps. A water blank can reveal contamination but must not be subtracted directly from pH, which is a logarithm.
The standards at pH 4, 7 and 10 do not bracket either endpoint of this protocol. Extreme readings therefore require independently checked instrument performance, and alkaline samples are sensitive to atmospheric carbon dioxide uptake. Electrode drift, incomplete mixing, volume error, dilution and changing ionic strength can shift apparent pKa values. A titration constrains the acid/base model; it cannot establish chirality or separate every microscopic protonation form. The two original diagrams show calculated predictions to compare with measured points, not reconstructed experimental data.

Chemical element

Words: 6k Articles: 199
Chemical substance OurBigBook.com
A chemical element is an identity shared by all chemical atoms whose atomic nuclei contain the same number of protons. That number is its atomic number, Z: six means carbon, eleven means sodium. The identity survives differences in neutron count, which distinguish isotopes, and differences in electron count, which distinguish neutral chemical atoms from ions. See the IUPAC Gold Book, chemical element.
The same name can also denote a pure chemical substance containing only that chemical element. These two uses answer different questions. Molecular oxygen, O2​, is a chemical substance made entirely of oxygen; water, H2​O, is a chemical compound containing both hydrogen and oxygen. A water molecule contains three chemical atoms but only two chemical elements. Joining chemical atoms through chemical bonds changes their arrangement without changing their atomic numbers.
This distinction makes stoichiometry possible: ordinary chemical reactions rearrange chemical atoms, so one can count each chemical element before and after a transformation. Changing the proton count instead changes the chemical element and requires a nuclear reaction. The periodic table organizes these identities into a useful map, while atomic number bookkeeping keeps identity, isotope, and electric charge separate.

Periodic table

Words: 555 Articles: 10
Chemical element OurBigBook.com
The periodic table arranges chemical elements in increasing atomic number, across successive periodic table periods. Its columns are periodic groups, numbered 1–18. The layout places recurring outer electron configurations above one another, making similarities in chemical bonds and chemical reactions easier to recognize. Ordering is by proton count, not by mass; the mass number of a particular isotope does not determine its box. See the official IUPAC periodic table and numbering conventions.
For the first eighteen neutral chemical atoms in their ground states, a compact description counts electrons in successive electron shells. Thus carbon has (2,4), meaning two electrons in the first electron shell and four in the second; the sum 2+4=6 agrees with its atomic number. Sodium has (2,8,1), whose sum is 11. These are occupancy counts, not circular trajectories of electrons.
Reading each row from left to right gives:
  • Periodic table period 1: hydrogen (1) and helium (2).
  • Periodic table period 2: lithium (2,1), beryllium (2,2), boron (2,3), carbon (2,4), nitrogen (2,5), oxygen (2,6), fluorine (2,7), and neon (2,8).
  • Periodic table period 3: sodium (2,8,1), magnesium (2,8,2), aluminium (2,8,3), silicon (2,8,4), phosphorus (2,8,5), sulfur (2,8,6), chlorine (2,8,7), and argon (2,8,8).
The counting outline is short: the occupied electron subshells in this range are 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, and 3p, filled in that order for these neutral ground states. Each s electron subshell holds up to two electrons and each p electron subshell up to six, giving 2, 2+6=8, and 2+6=8 along these three rows. This 2,8,8 summary applies only through argon; it is not a general rule that each electron shell fills completely before the next begins, nor a claim that the third electron shell can hold only eight electrons. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, electronic structure and electron configurations.
The recurring outer counts make the arrangement useful. Lithium and sodium each have one valence electron, whereas fluorine and chlorine each have seven valence electrons. Such similarities help anticipate chemical reactions, without making all properties identical throughout a periodic group. Helium is an instructive exception to an eight-electron shortcut: its two electrons complete the first electron shell, so it belongs above neon and argon in periodic group 18. Hydrogen shares column 1 with lithium and sodium but has its own distinct chemistry. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, periodic-table organization.

Its discovery shows why a small disagreement can matter more than a reassuringly repeatable result. Two preparations can each give consistent measurements while producing different mixtures. The Rayleigh-Ramsay argon density experiment investigated just such a discrepancy. Gas density links the weighing to a mean molar mass; a separate separation process tests which component accounts for it.

Rayleigh-Ramsay argon density experiment
Words: 218
Argon OurBigBook.com
In his 1895 lecture, Lord Rayleigh compared gas masses in a globe under matched pressure and temperature. Removing oxygen from air left gas about half a percent heavier than nitrogen prepared entirely from chemical sources. Several preparation routes reproduced the difference; hydrogen contamination was a concern. An eight-month storage test re-established the filling conditions: simply reweighing a sealed globe could not test a change in molar mass. William Ramsay concentrated the residual gas by circulating the mixture over hot magnesium, which consumed nitrogen. A spectral test checked remaining nitrogen. Agreement of spectra from this route and the alternative spark-and-alkali separation supported a common residual gas.[ref]
The density difference alone identifies neither a unique chemical element nor its concentration. A heavier contaminant, a lighter reference contaminant, or unmatched filling conditions can all shift a weighing. A separation process and an optical spectrum provide additional observations. This combination makes the experiment powerful: the anomaly motivates another operation whose result can be checked independently.
Argon detection in a binary gas mixture (x=MA​/MN​−1ρ/ρN​−1​)
Words: 300
Argon OurBigBook.com
Consider an original simplified model containing only nitrogen and argon, with argon mole fraction x. Let their molar masses be MN​ and MA​. Adding the component masses gives the mixture's mean molar mass
M=(1−x)MN​+xMA​.
(8)
For an ideal gas mixture at the same pressure and temperature as a pure-nitrogen reference, the gas density ratio is
r=ρN​ρ​=MN​M​=1+x(MN​MA​​−1),x=MA​/MN​−1r−1​.​
(9)
The inversion requires known identities, the binary-mixture assumption and MA​=MN​. A density ratio cannot uniquely recover an arbitrary multicomponent mixture. Nor should x be interpreted as the argon fraction of untreated air: the model sample has only the two specified components.
Choose round model values MN​=28gmol−1 and MA​=40gmol−1. For x=0.010, the calculated relative density excess is
r−1=0.010(2840​−1)=0.00428571…≃0.429%.​
(10)
Thus a one-percent mole fraction does not mean a one-percent gas density change. In a chosen 2.00L globe at 100kPa and 300K, the ideal gas law gives approximately 2.24508g for pure nitrogen and 2.25471g for this mixture: only 9.62mg separates the weighings. These are model calculations with rounded molar masses, not historical measurements.
A direct control calculation explains why the filling conditions matter. At fixed pressure, pure nitrogen at
T′=1+0.00428571…300K​≃298.720K
(11)
has the same gas density as that mixture at 300K. A roughly 1.28K mismatch can therefore imitate the entire stipulated composition signal. For small changes, the ideal gas law gives
ρdρ​=pdp​+MdM​−TdT​.
(12)
An independently measured pressure and temperature, matched weighing procedure, and checks for residual vapour distinguish composition from these alternative causes. The model explains the need for controls; it does not supply the complete corrections for a real gas-weighing instrument.

Atomic number (Z)

Words: 371
Chemical element OurBigBook.com
The atomic number Z is the number of protons in an atomic nucleus, and fixes the chemical element. It is a count, with no units. An atomic nucleus with six protons is always carbon, regardless of how many neutrons accompany them or how many electrons surround it. See the IUPAC Gold Book, atomic number.
Three independent bookkeeping questions become easy once their symbols are kept separate. Let N count neutrons, ne​ count electrons, A be the mass number, and Q be the net electric charge. A proton carries electric charge +e and an electron carries −e, where e is the positive elementary charge; a neutron carries zero net electric charge. Hence
A=Z+N,N=A−Z,Q=(Z−ne​)e,ne​=Z−Q/e.
(13)
The reasoning is just counting: add protons and neutrons for A, and subtract negative electron contributions from positive proton contributions for Q. A neutral chemical atom has Q=0, so ne​=Z. For a positively charged ion, fewer electrons remain. Notation ZA​X gives the mass number at upper left and atomic number at lower left, with X standing for the chemical element; a right superscript such as + specifies the electric charge in units of e. See Flowers et al., Chemistry 2e, atomic structure and symbolism.
For neutral carbon-12, 612​C, the atomic number gives six protons, the subtraction N=12−6=6 gives six neutrons, and neutrality gives six electrons. Neutral carbon-13, 613​C, instead has N=13−6=7 neutrons, with the same six protons and six electrons. Thus these two isotopes occupy the same carbon box in the periodic table.
For neutral sodium of mass number 23, 1123​Na, the counts are eleven protons, 23−11=12 neutrons, and eleven electrons. Removing one electron gives the ion 1123​Na+: Q/e=1, so ne​=11−1=10. Both its atomic number and its twelve neutrons stay unchanged. This is ionization, not conversion into the chemical element neon, even though a neutral neon chemical atom also has ten electrons.
This bookkeeping is useful whenever a symbol must be translated into a physical inventory. Mass number answers how many protons plus neutrons there are; electric charge answers the imbalance between protons and electrons; atomic number alone answers which chemical element it is. Keeping those questions distinct prevents an isotope or an ion from being mistaken for a different chemical element.

Isotope (ZA​X)

Words: 886 Articles: 14
Chemical element OurBigBook.com
Isotopes of a chemical element have the same atomic number Z, hence the same number of protons, but different neutron numbers N and therefore different mass numbers A=Z+N. For example, every neon atomic nucleus contains ten protons: neon-20, neon-21, and neon-22 contain ten, eleven, and twelve neutrons, respectively. They occupy one chemical element box in the periodic table, rather than three boxes.
Three labels answer different questions. The chemical element fixes Z; the isotope specifies which neutron number accompanies that Z; the ion label specifies the net electric charge. Neutral 1022​Ne and the ion 1022​Ne+ both contain ten protons and twelve neutrons; they contain ten and nine electrons, respectively. Ordinary ionization changes the electron count, leaving the isotope unchanged. Changing the neutron number can change nuclear binding energy and the possibility of radioactive decay. Isotopic abundances can help distinguish material sources, while radioactive decay can additionally supply chronological information.
A mass spectrum makes the distinction experimentally visible: a single chemical element can give separate ion peaks at different mass-to-charge ratios. Its bulk atomic weight is a weighted mean governed by isotopic abundances, rather than the location of one compulsory peak. The historical mass spectrograph experiment and the synthetic neon mass spectrum below illustrate these complementary observations.

The atomic mass of neutral carbon-12 in its ground state is exactly 12u by definition of the unified atomic mass unit. That exactness establishes the reference scale, rather than making the atomic masses of all isotopes exact integers in the same unit.

where the carbon-12 chemical atom is free, at rest, and in its nuclear and electronic ground state. Its conversion to SI mass units is determined experimentally. Nuclear mass defect (Δm=Zmp​+Nmn​−Mnuc​)
Words: 90
Atomic mass OurBigBook.com
The mass deficit of a bound atomic nucleus relative to its separated protons and neutrons. If their rest masses are mp​ and mn​, the atomic nucleus has rest mass Mnuc​, and the positive nuclear binding energy is B, then
Δm=Zmp​+Nmn​−Mnuc​=c2B​,
(16)
with c the speed of light. Releasing energy when the nucleons bind reduces the rest mass of the bound system without changing the exact count A=Z+N. A neutral atomic mass also includes Z electron rest masses, reduced by the energy required to separate those bound electrons. Consequently A−ma​/u is not the definition of the nuclear mass defect: the reference unit and constituent rest masses must also be accounted for.

An isotopic abundance is an atom fraction within a specified population of one chemical element.[ref] If ni​ counts its chemical atoms of isotope i, use
fi​=∑j​nj​ni​​,fi​≥0,∑i​fi​=1.

The denominator includes every isotope of that chemical element included in the stated population, not every chemical atom of every chemical element in the sample. Thus an oxygen atom fraction among all chemical elements is a different quantity.
For an illustrative neutral neon population, take the displayed central isotopic abundances f20​=0.9048, f21​=0.0027, and f22​=0.0925 from the reference table, so 0.9048+0.0027+0.0925=1. Its mean atomic mass is the weighted arithmetic mean
mˉ​=i∑​fi​mi​=(0.9048×19.9924401762+0.0027×20.993846685+0.0925×21.991385114)u=20.18004638052026u≈20.1800u.​
(18)
These are rounded reference inputs with uncertainties, not exact universal isotopic abundances; the long decimal shows their arithmetic result, not measurement precision.[ref]
The population convention matters. If instead wi​ is the fraction of total neutral-atom mass supplied by isotope i, then wi​=fi​mi​/mˉ and
mˉ=(∑i​mi​wi​​)−1.
(19)
This is a weighted harmonic mean in the mass fractions. Using ∑i​wi​mi​ with those mass fractions would answer a different question. The conversion follows directly by counting chemical atoms and adding their masses.

Carbon OurBigBook.com
Graphene is a single layer of carbon chemical atoms arranged in a honeycomb lattice. A nearby gate can select predominantly electron or electron hole conduction, as demonstrated by the graphene exfoliation and field-effect experiments.[ref]
A useful question is how geometry changes motion. The nearest-neighbour model of graphene starts with three equivalent bonds from each site and two sites per primitive cell. Interference between those three hopping paths makes two energy bands meet; near their meeting, energy grows linearly with distance in wave vector. The resulting Dirac cones explain why an atomic sheet can imitate one aspect of a relativistic particle while remaining an ordinary material with contacts, defects and boundaries.

Nearest-neighbour model of graphene (E±​(k)=±t∣f(k)∣)

Graphene OurBigBook.com
Take a planar honeycomb lattice with two sites A,B per primitive cell and one localized atomic orbital per site. In this explicitly idealized tight-binding model, all three nearest-neighbour hopping matrix elements are −t, with t>0; there is no on-site offset or further-neighbour hopping. Ignore electron interactions and treat physical spin as a separate degeneracy. Let the bond length be b, and choose the three vectors from an A site to its neighbours as
δ1​=b(0,1),δ2​=b(3​/2,−1/2),δ3​=b(−3​/2,−1/2).
(20)
The Bloch state amplitudes on A,B form a two-component vector. A consistent phase convention gives the Hamiltonian
H(k)=−t(0f(k)∗​f(k)0​),f(k)=∑j=13​eik⋅δj​=eibky​+2e−ibky​/2cos(3​bkx​/2).
(21)
Its characteristic equation is E2=t2∣f∣2, giving the two displayed energy bands. The two-component structure comes from the two sites, rather than two values of physical spin. This is a particularly small matrix model in which a crystal's geometry creates an unexpected low-energy law.
Historically, Philip Russell Wallace used a tight-binding model to investigate the electronic band structure of graphite in 1947. The material in that paper was layered graphite; the single-sheet model here isolates one simpler part of the problem.[ref]

Words: 293 Articles: 3
Nearest-neighbour model of graphene OurBigBook.com
At either displayed wave vector, the three complex hopping amplitudes add to zero: 1+2cos(2π/3)=0. Therefore the energy bands touch. There are two inequivalent electronic valleys; other equivalent corners are related by reciprocal-lattice translations. Setting k=Kτ​+q and retaining first-order terms gives
Hτ​(q)≃ℏvF​(τqx​σx​+qy​σy​),vF​=2ℏ3tb​,E±​≃±ℏvF​∣q∣,
(22)
where σx​,σy​ are Pauli matrices. For example, at K+​, f≃−3b(qx​−iqy​)/2. The matrix has the form of a massless two-dimensional Dirac Hamiltonian. Here vF​ is a material-model velocity, rather than the vacuum speed of light; this description does not change an electron's vacuum rest mass. It describes the dispersion relation of electronic excitations near a band crossing.

At K+​ and positive energy, a normalized eigenvector for q=∣q∣(cosϕ,sinϕ) is (1,eiϕ)/2​. Its Pauli matrix expectation values give the displayed direction. This pseudospin records the relative amplitudes and phase on the two sublattices. Real spin supplies another label; confusing these two labels would double-count states and misinterpret the two-band Hamiltonian.

Words: 85
Dirac valleys in graphene OurBigBook.com
Assume zero temperature, the linear Dirac cone, and both real-spin states and both electronic valleys. Define n as excess electron number per unit area, negative for an excess of electron holes, relative to neutrality. A filled circular region of radius kF​ in wave vector space contains
∣n∣=4(2π)2πkF2​​=πkF2​​,∣EF​∣=ℏvF​kF​.
(23)
Thus the excess carrier density grows quadratically with the Fermi energy, unlike the constant density of states of a parabolic two-dimensional band. Differentiating gives the positive density of states per unit area, D(E)=2∣E∣/[π(ℏvF​)2]. Both the geometry of occupied states and the fourfold degeneracy matter to the coefficient.

Words: 59
Dirac valleys in graphene OurBigBook.com
A massless-cone description permits a nonzero cyclotron effective mass. For a circular constant-energy contour of area S(E)=πE2/(ℏvF​)2, the semiclassical definition gives
mc​=2πℏ2​​dEdS​​=vF2​∣EF​∣​=vF​ℏπ∣n∣​​.
(24)
The vanishing mass parameter in a Dirac Hamiltonian and the finite cyclotron response away from neutrality are different statements. This makes the temperature dependence of Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations a useful test of the dispersion rather than a measurement of an electron's vacuum rest mass.
Graphene exfoliation and field-effect experiments (2004–2005)
Words: 129
Graphene OurBigBook.com
Andre Geim, Konstantin Novoselov and collaborators mechanically cleaved graphite, identified thin flakes, and fabricated multi-terminal Hall bars on oxidized silicon. A substrate gate changed the carrier density; longitudinal electrical resistance and the Hall coefficient supplied different checks. The 2004 report included one-, two- and three-layer devices and described a few-layer semimetal interpretation. Layer identification and electrical control were separate experimental achievements.[ref]
The 2005 monolayer study used an optical microscope, electron microscopy and atomic force microscopy to select monolayers. It then measured Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations as temperature, gate voltage and magnetic field varied. Their damping inferred a density-dependent cyclotron effective mass; comparison with oscillation frequency tested a linear dispersion relation. A comparison with two-layer devices also distinguished their quantum Hall effect sequences. These are complementary tests of the monolayer model, rather than consequences of finding a thin-looking flake alone.[ref]
Gate control of graphene carrier density (Vg​−V0​=en/cg​+EF​/e)
Words: 305 Articles: 1
Graphene OurBigBook.com
Consider an ideal uniform graphene sheet connected to an electron reservoir, with an insulated gate. Let cg​>0 be geometric capacitance per unit area, e>0 the elementary charge, and V0​ the neutral-point offset. Neglect temperature, trapped electric charge and spatial inhomogeneity. A change in gate voltage pays for both the electrostatic potential drop, en/cg​, and the change in the sheet's Fermi energy, EF​/e. Here EF​ is measured relative to the band crossing; it is negative for excess electron holes.
Combine this relation with the carrier density in a graphene cone. Write u=∣EF​∣/e, measured in volts, V=∣Vg​−V0​∣, and α=e3/[π(ℏvF​)2cg​]. Then
V=u+αu2,u=1+1+4αV​2V​,n=sgn(Vg​−V0​)π(ℏvF​)2e2u2​.
(25)
The positive root is unique because u+αu2 is strictly increasing for u≥0. The often useful geometric approximation n≃cg​(Vg​−V0​)/e neglects the Fermi energy term. It overestimates ∣n∣ in this model, especially near neutrality where relatively few states are available.
For a deliberately chosen model with cg​=0.010F/m2, vF​=106m/s, V0​=0 and Vg​=1V, the formulas give EF​≃0.252eV and n≃4.67×1012cm−2. The purely geometric value would be 6.24×1012cm−2. These are chosen-model predictions, not measurements of the historical devices. Numerical conversion uses the exact Planck constant and elementary charge.[ref]

The quantum capacitance per unit area is cq​=e2D(EF​). Differentiating the gate equation gives
cdiff​1​=cg​1​+cq​1​,cdiff​=edVg​dn​.
(26)
Thus the available electronic states act as a second contribution in series with geometric capacitance. At exact neutrality the ideal zero-temperature model has cq​=cdiff​=0; actual finite-temperature or spatially nonuniform samples need a broader description. A capacitance measurement can therefore probe the density of states, rather than geometry alone.

Tropospheric ozone

Words: 326 Articles: 7
Ozone OurBigBook.com
Ozone in the troposphere is a secondary chemical pollutant and a radiatively active gas. Its abundance reflects photochemical production, chemical loss, dry deposition and transport. The photodissociation of nitrogen dioxide alone is part of a null ozone cycle unless peroxy radicals regenerate nitrogen dioxide without consuming ozone.
Ozone titration
Words: 30
Tropospheric ozone OurBigBook.com
Local ozone consumption by the reaction NO+O3​→NO2​+O2​. Reducing fresh NO emissions can raise local measured ozone even while decreasing regional ozone production. This distinction matters when interpreting precursor-control experiments and observations.
Photochemical ozone production
Words: 261 Articles: 5
Tropospheric ozone OurBigBook.com
Net daylight ozone production occurs when peroxy radicals oxidize NO to NO2 without using ozone, followed by NO2 photodissociation and oxygen-atom addition to O2. The competing reaction NO + O3 to NO2 + O2 only recycles odd oxygen. Radical initiation, termination, precursor loading and transport determine the net rate.
VOC-limited ozone production
Words: 42
Photochemical ozone production OurBigBook.com
A regime in which precursor/radical supply and NOx-dependent radical termination make net ozone production more responsive to additional reactive organic compounds than to additional nitrogen oxides. Reducing nitrogen oxides can initially raise ozone in some such conditions. Diagnose the chemical regime before extrapolating an emission reduction to every location.
NOx-limited ozone production
Words: 30
Photochemical ozone production OurBigBook.com
A regime in which additional available nitrogen oxides tends to increase net photochemical ozone production when other factors are fixed. Reducing nitrogen oxides generally suppresses that production, but local ozone concentration also depends on transport, deposition and NO titration.
Ozone isopleth diagram
Words: 54
Photochemical ozone production OurBigBook.com
A contour plot of a specified ozone outcome against the loadings of nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds. The ridge separating opposite NOx sensitivities distinguishes an NOx-limited ozone-production regime from a VOC-limited ozone-production regime. The outcome may be peak concentration, a time-integrated measure or a model production rate; axes and averaging conditions must be stated. A schematic diagram is not a calibrated emissions-response prediction.
VOC-limited ozone-production regime
Words: 47
Photochemical ozone production OurBigBook.com
A regime with abundant nitrogen oxides in which volatile-organic oxidation and radical supply limit net tropospheric ozone production. Reducing volatile organic compounds lowers production. A small NOx reduction can initially increase ozone by weakening OH termination and NO titration; sufficiently large reductions can cross into an NOx-limited ozone-production regime. Local concentration and regional emission sensitivities need not coincide.
NOx-limited ozone-production regime (NOx​)
Words: 43
Photochemical ozone production OurBigBook.com
A regime in which additional nitrogen oxides promote net tropospheric ozone production because NO availability limits peroxy-radical oxidation of NO. Reducing NOx then generally lowers ozone production, subject to transport and chemical history. At much larger NOx burdens, OH removal by nitric-acid formation can instead produce a VOC-limited ozone-production regime.
